title: Abbreviation
directAnswer: Decide whether string `a` can be turned into the all-uppercase string `b` using only two moves: capitalize zero or more lowercase letters of `a`, and delete the remaining lowercase letters. Uppercase letters in `a` are frozen — they can neither be deleted nor changed. This is a two-sequence subsequence-matching DP: dp[i][j] = can the first i characters of a produce the first j characters of b. A lowercase a[i-1] may be deleted (carry dp[i-1][j]) or capitalized to match b[j-1] (take dp[i-1][j-1]); an uppercase a[i-1] MUST match b[j-1] exactly. O(n·m) time and space.

remember.formula:
dp[0][0] = true
for i in 1..n, j in 0..m:
    if a[i-1] is UPPERCASE:
        dp[i][j] = (j>0 && a[i-1]==b[j-1]) ? dp[i-1][j-1] : false
    else  # lowercase
        dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j]                       # delete a[i-1]
                   || (j>0 && upper(a[i-1])==b[j-1]  # OR capitalize it
                        && dp[i-1][j-1])
answer = dp[n][m]
rules: `b` is **always all uppercase** — every character of `b` must be produced by either keeping an uppercase letter of `a` or capitalizing a lowercase one.
An **uppercase** letter in `a` is non-negotiable: it cannot be deleted, so if it doesn't line up with the current `b` character the path dies.
A **lowercase** letter in `a` is a free agent: delete it (move down a row, same column) or capitalize it to consume a `b` character (move diagonally) — only if it uppercases to that character.
Iterate `j` from **0**, not 1: the `j == 0` column answers 'can a[0..i-1] vanish entirely?', which is true only while every letter seen is lowercase.
Compare `Character.toUpperCase(a[i-1]) == b[j-1]`, never `a[i-1] == b[j-1]` for the lowercase branch — you're matching the *capitalized* form.
whenToUse: Two strings, asking 'can one transform into the other' under per-character keep/delete/transform rules
One string is a constrained subsequence of the other after a case or filter operation
Characters split into 'mutable' and 'frozen' classes with different allowed moves
A yes/no reachability question over a 2D (prefix-of-a, prefix-of-b) state
antiSignals: You need the minimum number of edits, not a yes/no → Edit Distance (numeric DP)
Both strings are freely editable with insert as well → classic LCS / edit-distance family
Single string, no second target → 1D DP, not this grid
Wildcards `?`/`*` rather than case rules → Wildcard Matching
remember.takeaway: Abbreviation is Edit Distance's boolean cousin: the same prefix-by-prefix grid, but each cell is reachable-or-not instead of a cost, and the allowed moves are dictated by the *case* of the current character. Split characters into mutable (lowercase) and frozen (uppercase) and the recurrence writes itself.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you model an asymmetric transform (lowercase = delete-or-capitalize, uppercase = must-match) as a 2D boolean reachability DP rather than greedy character matching.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to match greedily left-to-right (capitalize whenever it fits) — this fails because sometimes a lowercase letter that *could* match must instead be deleted so a later letter can match. Also forgetting that an unmatched uppercase letter in `a` makes the whole thing impossible.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name it as a subsequence/edit-distance-style grid, derive the two branches from the case of the character, handle the j=0 column explicitly, then note the O(m)-space rolling-row optimization.

problemStatement:
You are given two strings, `a` and `b`. You can perform the following operations on string `a`:

1. **Capitalize** zero or more of `a`'s lowercase letters.
2. **Delete** all of the remaining lowercase letters in `a`.

Given `a` and `b`, determine whether it is possible to make `a` **equal to** `b` using these operations. Note that `b` consists only of uppercase letters, and the uppercase letters already present in `a` can be neither deleted nor altered.

Return `"YES"` if `a` can be transformed into `b`, otherwise `"NO"`.
constraints: `a` consists of uppercase and lowercase English letters
`b` consists only of uppercase English letters
Uppercase letters in `a` cannot be deleted or changed
Lowercase letters in `a` may each be capitalized or deleted
understanding: Think of walking through `a` once. Each lowercase letter offers a fork: capitalize it (and it must then equal the next needed letter of `b`) or throw it away. Each uppercase letter is fixed — it has to be the next needed letter of `b`, or the attempt is doomed. The question is whether some sequence of these forced and free choices reproduces `b` exactly.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is `b` guaranteed to be all uppercase?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. That's why every `b` character must come from a kept-uppercase or a capitalized-lowercase letter of `a`.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I delete uppercase letters in `a` that don't appear in `b`?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — uppercase letters are frozen. A leftover uppercase letter in `a` with nothing to match in `b` immediately forces 'NO'.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must lowercase letters that happen to match `b` be capitalized?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, and that's the trap. A lowercase letter may need to be *deleted* even when capitalizing it would match, so a later letter can line up. That non-greedy choice is exactly what the DP explores.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if |a| < |b|?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Then it's impossible — you can never produce more target characters than `a` has letters to supply. The DP returns false naturally, but you can short-circuit.

examples.explanation: Delete the first 'd', capitalize 'a'→'A', keep 'B', capitalize 'c'→'C', delete the last 'd'. Result: "ABC".
After keeping 'A', the next needed letter is 'F'. The only lowercase letters available are 'b' and 'c', which capitalize to 'B'/'C', never 'F'. No way to produce 'F'.
Keep 'A', capitalize 'b'→'B', delete 'c', keep 'D', keep 'E'. Result: "ABDE".

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recurse on Capitalize / Delete
approaches.whenToMention: State it first to reveal the two branches and the overlapping subproblems, then add memoization or a table.
hints: Walk a pointer i over `a` and j over `b`. At each step, what can you do with a[i] depending on whether it's upper or lowercase?

If a[i] is lowercase you branch: either capitalize it (only legal when it uppercases to b[j], then advance both) or delete it (advance i only). If a[i] is uppercase it must equal b[j] to advance both, else this path fails.
Base cases: if j reached the end of b, the rest of a must be all lowercase (deletable). If i reached the end of a but j hasn't, fail.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each lowercase character can branch two ways, giving up to 2ⁿ leaf paths; recursion depth is O(n) for the call stack.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal reading: try to consume `b` one character at a time while scanning `a`. Maintain two indices, `i` into `a` and `j` into `b`.

**The branches.** If `a[i]` is lowercase, you have a genuine choice. You may *capitalize* it — but only if `toUpper(a[i]) == b[j]` — which consumes `b[j]` and advances both pointers. Or you may *delete* it, advancing only `i`. If `a[i]` is uppercase, there is no choice: it must equal `b[j]` (advance both); if it doesn't, this path is impossible.

**Why it must branch (greedy fails).** Consider `a = "Aa", b = "A"`. Greedily capitalizing the lowercase 'a' would over-produce; you must *delete* it instead. Conversely sometimes you must capitalize even though deleting looks simpler. Because a lowercase letter that *could* match might need to be deleted to let a later letter match, you cannot commit greedily — you explore both forks.

**Base cases.** When `j == m` (all of `b` produced), success requires every remaining character of `a` to be lowercase (so they can be deleted); a leftover uppercase letter forces failure. When `i == n` but `j < m`, you've run out of letters to supply `b` → failure.

**Why we don't ship this.** Every lowercase letter doubles the path count, so the tree is `2ⁿ`. But the only thing that distinguishes a subproblem is the pair `(i, j)`, and there are just `n·m` such pairs — the same states are recomputed exponentially often. That redundancy is the cue to memoize.
approaches.insight: There are only n·m distinct (i, j) states but exponentially many paths reach them. Caching each (i, j) the first time collapses 2ⁿ into n·m — the universal DP trigger of 'few states, recomputed often'.

java.explanation: All of b produced — success only if every remaining char of a is lowercase (deletable).

Capitalize branch is legal only when the uppercased letter equals b[j].
Either fork succeeding is enough — this OR is why greedy can't replace the recursion.

python.line: return all(not a[k].isupper() for k in range(i, len(a)))
python.explanation: Leftover uppercase letters can't be deleted → they kill an otherwise-complete match.
Frozen letter: no choice, must line up with b[j].

python.line: capitalize = ca.upper() == b[j] and solve(i + 1, j + 1)
python.explanation: Only capitalize when the result actually matches the needed b character.
Explore both forks for lowercase letters.

diagrams.title: Recursion forks on every lowercase letter
diagrams.caption: The same (i, j) state can be reached on multiple paths — the exponential waste.

pitfalls: Forgetting to verify leftover characters are lowercase when j hits the end of b.
Allowing the capitalize branch when toUpper(a[i]) != b[j] — an illegal move.
Running it on |a| = 1000 — 2ⁿ never returns; memoize or tabulate.

approaches.name: 2D Boolean DP — Tabulation (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'an edit-distance-style grid where each cell is reachable-or-not'.
hints: Define dp[i][j] = can the first i characters of a be transformed into the first j characters of b? You want dp[n][m].
dp[0][0] = true (empty produces empty). Fill the j=0 column: dp[i][0] is true only while a[0..i-1] is all lowercase (everything deletable).
Transition by the case of a[i-1]: uppercase forces dp[i][j] = (a[i-1]==b[j-1]) && dp[i-1][j-1]; lowercase allows delete (dp[i-1][j]) OR capitalize (dp[i-1][j-1] when upper(a[i-1])==b[j-1]).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Exactly (n+1)(m+1) cells, each filled in O(1) → O(n·m) time. The full table is O(n·m) space.
approaches.explanation:
Turn the recursion inside-out. Let `dp[i][j]` mean *'the first `i` characters of `a` can be transformed into the first `j` characters of `b`'*. The answer is `dp[n][m]`.

**Initialization.** `dp[0][0] = true` — an empty prefix of `a` trivially yields an empty prefix of `b`. The first column `dp[i][0]` asks 'can `a[0..i-1]` be deleted entirely?'. That's true only if every one of those characters is lowercase, so `dp[i][0] = dp[i-1][0] && isLowercase(a[i-1])`. The first row `dp[0][j>0]` is false: nothing can produce a non-empty `b`.

**Transition — uppercase a[i-1].** A frozen letter can only be kept, and only if it equals the target: `dp[i][j] = (a[i-1] == b[j-1]) && dp[i-1][j-1]`. If they differ, the cell is false.

**Transition — lowercase a[i-1].** Two ways to reach `dp[i][j]`:
- *Delete* `a[i-1]`: the target prefix is unchanged, so inherit `dp[i-1][j]`.
- *Capitalize* `a[i-1]` to consume `b[j-1]`: legal only when `toUpper(a[i-1]) == b[j-1]`, contributing `dp[i-1][j-1]`.

Combine with OR: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] || (toUpper(a[i-1]) == b[j-1] && dp[i-1][j-1])`.

**Why iterate j from 0.** The `j == 0` column carries the 'delete everything so far' state. If you start `j` at 1 you lose the ability to delete a prefix of `a` before the first `b` character is matched — and `a = "xY", b = "Y"` would wrongly fail.

**Why this is correct and fast.** Every (i, j) state is computed exactly once from already-filled neighbours above and to the upper-left, so there's no recomputation. `n·m ≤ 10⁶` cells for the constraints — instant.
approaches.insight: The grid is identical in shape to Edit Distance and LCS; only the cell semantics change from 'cost' to 'reachable'. Recognising that lets you reuse the same loop skeleton and just swap the recurrence body — case-of-character decides the move set.

edgeCases.behavior: Keep 'P', delete lowercase 'i' → dp[2][1] inherits dp[1][1]=T → YES.

pitfalls: Starting the j loop at 1 — loses the delete-the-prefix state in column 0.
Comparing a[i-1] == b[j-1] in the lowercase branch instead of toUpper(a[i-1]) == b[j-1].
Forgetting that an uppercase letter that doesn't match simply leaves the cell false (never OR-in a delete for it).

approaches.name: Rolling-Row DP — O(m) Space
approaches.whenToMention: Mention after the 2D table as the memory-tightening step when |a| can be large.
hints: dp[i][*] depends only on dp[i-1][*]. Do you ever read a row older than the previous one?
Keep two 1D arrays, prev and cur, of length m+1. Compute cur from prev each row, then swap.
Watch the j=0 cell of cur: it must encode 'a[0..i-1] all lowercase', so set it before the inner loop based on prev[0] and the case of a[i-1].
approaches.complexityReasoning: Still (n+1)(m+1) cell computations → O(n·m) time, but only two rows of length m+1 are retained → O(m) space.
approaches.explanation:
The tabulation only ever reads the immediately previous row, so storing all `n+1` rows is wasteful. Keep `prev` (row `i-1`) and `cur` (row `i`).

**Handling column 0 per row.** `cur[0]` answers 'can `a[0..i-1]` be entirely deleted?', which is `prev[0] && isLowercase(a[i-1])`. Set this before the inner loop because the lowercase delete branch reads `cur`'s own column-0 lineage indirectly through `prev`.

**The inner loop** is identical to the 2D version with `dp[i-1][j] → prev[j]` and `dp[i-1][j-1] → prev[j-1]`. After finishing the row, swap `prev` and `cur` (and clear `cur`).

**Why ship it when |a| is large.** With `|a|, |b| ≤ 1000` the full table is only ~10⁶ booleans — fine. But the O(m) version generalises better and demonstrates you see the bounded look-back. The trade-off: you lose the full table, so you can't reconstruct *which* letters were capitalised vs deleted without extra bookkeeping.
approaches.insight: A DP whose recurrence reads only the previous row collapses from O(n·m) to O(m) space by alternating two rows. The same trick shrinks LCS, Edit Distance, and 0/1 Knapsack — recognise the single-row look-back and the optimisation is mechanical.

diagrams.caption: Only prev and cur exist at any time; cur becomes prev each iteration.

edgeCases.behavior: m=0; prev[0] stays true through all lowercase rows → YES (delete everything).
Row 'X' sets cur[0] = false (uppercase can't be deleted) → NO.

pitfalls: Reusing a single array in place — reading already-overwritten cur[j-1] corrupts the row; use separate prev/cur.
Forgetting to recompute cur[0] each row — it changes the moment an uppercase letter appears.
Expecting to recover the capitalize/delete choices — O(m) space discards the witness.

commonMistakes: Matching greedily — capitalizing every lowercase letter that fits, which can block a later required match.
Forgetting that leftover uppercase letters in `a` (with no target in `b`) make the answer NO.
Starting the inner loop at j=1, losing the 'delete the whole prefix' state in column 0.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Greedy capitalize instead of branching
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On a = "Aa", b = "A": greedily capitalizing the lowercase 'a' produces "AA" ≠ "A". You must delete it. Only branching (or the DP's OR) captures this.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Ignoring leftover uppercase letters
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When b is exhausted, any remaining uppercase letter in a is undeletable, so the match fails. Returning true unconditionally at j==m is wrong.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: if (j == b.length()) return true;  // ignores leftover uppercase in a

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing wrong case in lowercase branch
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A lowercase letter matches b[j-1] only after capitalization, so you must compare toUpper(a[i-1]), not a[i-1] itself.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: if (ca == b.charAt(j - 1)) dp[i][j] |= dp[i-1][j-1];  // never true: ca is lowercase

followupVariations.title: Edit Distance
followupVariations.hint: Same prefix-by-prefix grid, but cells hold minimum cost (insert/delete/replace) instead of a boolean.

followupVariations.title: Wildcard Matching
followupVariations.hint: 2D boolean DP again, where '*' and '?' set the legal moves instead of letter case.

followupVariations.title: Longest Common Subsequence
followupVariations.hint: The numeric ancestor of this grid — match consumes both indices, mismatch takes the better neighbour.

followupVariations.title: Distinct Subsequences
followupVariations.hint: Count (not yes/no) the ways one string forms another as a subsequence — the same grid with addition replacing OR.

patternNote: Two-sequence boolean reachability DP — Edit Distance's grid with reachable-or-not cells. The case of each character of `a` selects the move set: lowercase = delete or capitalize, uppercase = forced match. Recognise it whenever a transform question pits a 'mutable' character class against a 'frozen' one over two strings.
